grammar.title: Can / could / be able to
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Can** = habilidade **presente** (saber, conseguir, poder):
"I **can** speak three languages." / "**Can** you swim?"

**Could** = habilidade **geral no passado**:
"I **could** read when I was five." / "I **couldn't** sleep last night."

**Be able to** = o mesmo sentido de can, mas funciona em **todos os tempos**, onde can não pode ir:
- futuro: "I**'ll be able to** come tomorrow." (❌ "I'll can")
- present perfect: "I**'ve never been able to** whistle." (❌ "I've could")
- depois de outro verbo: "I'd like **to be able to** play the piano."

**Sucesso numa situação específica do passado:** use **was able to** ou **managed to** (não could):
"The fire was huge, but everyone **was able to** escape." / "I **managed to** finish on time."
Na negativa, **couldn't** funciona sempre: "I **couldn't** find my keys."

**Perguntas com How:** How **fast** can you run? How **long** can you hold your breath? How **well** can you cook? How **far** can you swim?

listening.title: Amazing animals
listening.context_pt: Trecho de um documentário sobre habilidades incríveis de animais.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.en: Animals can do incredible things. A cheetah can run at more than one hundred kilometers per hour, but only for about thirty seconds. A sperm whale can hold its breath for ninety minutes and dive more than two kilometers deep. Some parrots can learn hundreds of words, and one famous parrot, Alex, was able to identify colors and shapes. And the tiny tardigrade? Scientists have discovered that it can survive in space, without water or oxygen. Humans, on the other hand, can't run very fast or hold their breath for long — but we can do something no animal can: we can tell stories about all of them.

reading.title: It's never too late
reading.text: Many adults believe that they can't learn new skills after a certain age. "I couldn't learn a language now — my brain is too old," they say. Neuroscience says otherwise. Thanks to neuroplasticity, our brains can create new connections throughout our lives. Children may learn some things faster, but adults have advantages too: they can organize their study, understand grammar rules and connect new information to what they already know. Consider Dona Neusa from Minas Gerais: she couldn't read until she was 70. She went back to school, and two years later she was able to read her first novel. "I've been able to do things I never imagined," she says. Her secret? "I never gave up."

grammar.title: Pedidos e How could you...?
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Escala de educação dos pedidos:**
1. **Can you** + verbo? → informal, amigos e família
2. **Could you** + verbo? → educado, o mais versátil
3. **Would you** + verbo? → educado
4. **Would you mind** + verbo-**ing**? → muito educado (bom para favores grandes)
5. **I was wondering if you could** + verbo → muito indireto e formal

Para pedidos grandes, **prepare o terreno**: "Could you do me a **big** favor?" / "I hate to ask, but..."

**Respostas:**
- Sim: Sure! / Of course. / No problem. / I'd be happy to.
- Não (com educação): I'm sorry, I can't. I... / I'd love to help, but... / I'm afraid I'm busy.

**How could you...?** = Como você pôde...? (indignação ou surpresa no passado)
"**How could you** leave your keys at home **again**?!"

**Why couldn't you...?** = Por que você não conseguiu / não pôde...?
"**Why couldn't you** call me earlier?"

reading.title: The Ben Franklin effect
reading.text: Do you want someone to like you more? Ask them for a favor. It sounds strange, but it's a well-known psychological phenomenon called the Ben Franklin effect. In the 18th century, Benjamin Franklin had a political rival who didn't like him. Instead of being extra nice to him, Franklin wrote a polite letter asking if he could borrow a rare book from the man's library. The rival lent it, Franklin returned it with a warm thank-you note, and the two became friends. Psychologists explain that when we do someone a favor, our brain looks for a reason: "I helped this person, so I must like them." The lesson? Small favors — "Could you recommend a good restaurant?" — can build relationships. Just don't ask for too many!

questions.q: How do psychologists explain the effect?
questions.answer: Our brain thinks: "I helped this person, so I must like them."

questions.q: What is the warning at the end?
questions.answer: Don't ask for too many favors.

grammar.title: Conselhos: should, ought to, had better
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Should / shouldn't** + verbo base → conselho, opinião (o mais comum):
"You **should** see a doctor." / "You **shouldn't** work so late." / "**Should** I call him?"

**Ought to** + verbo base → mesmo sentido de should, um pouco mais formal e menos comum em perguntas e negativas:
"You **ought to** apologize."

**Had better ('d better)** + verbo base → conselho **forte, com aviso** de consequência negativa (é presente/futuro, apesar do "had"):
"You**'d better** leave now, **or** you'll miss your flight."
Negativa: "You**'d better not** tell her."

**Outras formas de aconselhar:**
- **If I were you, I'd** + verbo → "If I were you, I'd take the job." (note: **were** para todas as pessoas)
- **Why don't you** + verbo? → "Why don't you try yoga?"
- **Have you tried** + -ing? → "Have you tried meditating?"
- **I'd recommend** + -ing → "I'd recommend talking to HR."

Lembre-se: **advice** é incontável → "some advice", "a piece of advice" (❌ "an advice", "advices").

reading.title: Advice from 100-year-olds
reading.text: What can we learn from people who have lived for a century? Journalists and researchers who have interviewed centenarians around the world have noticed some common advice. "You shouldn't worry so much about money — you can't take it with you," said a 102-year-old woman from Okinawa, Japan. A former farmer from Sardinia, Italy, recommended: "Walk every day, and eat with your family." Many said that people ought to forgive more easily, because holding grudges only hurts yourself. And almost all of them mentioned relationships: "If I were you, I'd call my friends more often. In the end, people are what matter." Interestingly, very few of them talked about work or success. Maybe we'd better listen to them before it's too late.

Dear Confused,
First of all, congratulations on the offer! It's completely normal to feel divided. Here's my advice. grammar.title: must / have to / mustn't / don't have to + might / may
grammar.explanation_pt:
**OBRIGAÇÃO**
- **Must** + verbo → obrigação forte, regras escritas, ou algo que **você** acha necessário: "Passengers **must** wear seatbelts." / "I **must** call my mom."
- **Have to** + verbo → obrigação externa, do dia a dia (regras, circunstâncias). É mais comum na fala e funciona em todos os tempos: "I **have to** work on Saturday." / "She **has to** wear a uniform." / "I **had to** wait for an hour." / "You'll **have to** pay a fine."

**⚠️ A grande pegadinha das negativas:**
- **mustn't** = **proibido** (não pode!): "You **mustn't** use your phone while driving."
- **don't have to** = **não precisa** (é opcional): "You **don't have to** wear a tie. It's casual Friday."

**POSSIBILIDADE (talvez)**
- **might / may / could** + verbo = pode ser que, talvez: "It **might** rain." / "She **may** be late." / "That **could** be a problem."
- Negativa: **might not / may not** (não could not): "I **might not** go."

**DEDUÇÃO (tenho quase certeza)**
- **must be** = deve ser (certeza positiva): "You worked 12 hours? You **must be** exhausted!"
- **can't be** = não pode ser (certeza negativa): "That **can't be** Ana — she's in Paris."

rows: You have to show your ID.
You don't have to pay. It's free.

grammar.tip_pt: **Must** não tem passado. Para obrigação no passado, use **had to**: "Yesterday I **had to** work late" (❌ "I musted").

common_mistakes.wrong: You mustn't come to the party if you're tired. (querendo dizer "não precisa")
common_mistakes.right: You don't have to come to the party if you're tired.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Mustn't = proibido. "Não precisa" = don't have to.

common_mistakes.right: I must go now. / I have to go now.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Must + verbo base, sem to (mas have to tem to!).

common_mistakes.right: Yesterday I had to work late.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **Have to** soa "**réfta**" (com F!), **has to** = "**résta**", **had to** = "**rétta**". **Mustn't** = "mâsent" — o primeiro T é mudo. **Might** = "máit", com T leve.

reading.title: Strange laws around the world
reading.text: Every country has its rules, but some laws might surprise you. In Singapore, you mustn't chew gum in most situations — selling it has been illegal since 1992 to keep the streets clean. In Switzerland, some apartment buildings have rules saying residents mustn't flush the toilet late at night because of the noise. In Japan, companies with employees aged 40 to 74 have to measure their waists during health checks — a policy to fight obesity. In Denmark, parents must choose their babies' names from an official list of approved names, or ask for special permission. These laws might seem strange, but each one tells us something about the culture that created it.
